title: Chart for a 24-month trend
question: A product manager wants to show how monthly active users changed over the last 24 months so the audience can spot growth and seasonality. Which chart fits best?
options: A pie chart with one slice per month
A line chart with months on the x-axis
A scatter plot of users against revenue
A treemap sized by each month's users
explanation: Line charts connect ordered points along a continuous time axis, which makes direction, slope and seasonal patterns easy to read. A pie chart with 24 slices hides the order and makes small differences unreadable, a treemap shows part-to-whole without the time sequence, and a scatter plot of users versus revenue answers a correlation question, not a trend question.

title: Showing the distribution of order values
question: An analyst needs to show how the values of 50,000 orders are distributed, including skew and unusually large orders. Which chart should they choose?
options: A bar chart of the ten largest orders
A line chart of order values sorted by order ID
A pie chart with one slice per sales channel
A histogram that bins order values into ranges
explanation: A histogram groups a numeric measure into bins and plots how many records fall into each one, revealing shape, skew, gaps and outliers. The top-ten bar chart only shows the extreme tail, ordering by order ID imposes a meaningless sequence, and the pie chart breaks down a different dimension instead of showing the distribution of values.

title: Bar chart with a truncated value axis
question: A bar chart compares revenue for two regions: A has $0.98M and B has $1.02M. The value axis starts at $960K, so B's bar looks three times taller than A's. What is the best correction?
options: Start the axis at zero, or use a dot plot if small gaps matter
Switch the value axis to a logarithmic scale to compress the gap
Render the bars in 3D so the depth hints at the real proportions
Sort the bars alphabetically so the comparison feels more neutral
explanation: Bars encode value by length, so a non-zero baseline exaggerates differences: here a gap of about 4% looks like a threefold difference. Starting at zero restores honest proportions, and if the small gap is the point, a dot plot (which encodes by position, not length) can use a tighter axis. A log scale distorts the comparison differently, 3D adds perspective distortion, and sorting does nothing about the misleading lengths.

title: Filled map that only mirrors population
question: A filled (choropleth) map colors each state by its total number of support tickets. The darkest states are simply the most populous ones, and the team wants to find where customers struggle most. What should change?
options: Switch to a rainbow palette so the mid-range states stand out more
Increase the number of color steps so that every state gets its own shade
Color by a rate, e.g. tickets per 1,000 customers, not the raw count
Extrude the states in 3D so ticket volume is shown as height as well
explanation: Area-colored maps of raw totals mostly reproduce the population map, because big states have more of everything. Normalizing to a rate (per customer, per capita) makes states comparable and reveals where the problem is actually concentrated. Rainbow palettes and extra shades do not fix the wrong measure, and 3D extrusion adds occlusion without addressing it.

title: Reading a crossing point on a dual-axis chart
question: A combo chart plots revenue (left axis, $) and churn rate (right axis, %). In Q3 the two lines cross, and an executive concludes that 'churn overtook revenue'. What is the correct reading?
options: The crossing is an artifact of two independent scales and means nothing
Churn overtook revenue, since both lines share the same plotting area
The crossing is the break-even point where churn costs equal revenue
The reading is valid as long as the right axis also starts at zero
explanation: Each axis on a dual-axis chart is scaled independently, so where the lines cross or which one sits higher depends only on how the two axes were scaled; rescaling either axis can move the intersection anywhere. A currency and a percentage share no unit, so neither an 'overtaking' nor a break-even reading is valid, and aligning the zeros does not create a common unit either.

title: Where to place the most important metric
question: You are laying out a dashboard for an audience that reads left-to-right, top-to-bottom. Where should the single most important, highest-level metric go?
options: Bottom-right, as the conclusion the reader reaches last
In the center, surrounded by the supporting detail visuals
Top-left, with more detail following in reading order
On a separate page opened from a button on the dashboard
explanation: People scan a page in their reading direction, so the top-left corner gets attention first; Microsoft's dashboard guidance recommends putting the highest-level data there and adding detail as the eye moves right and down. Placing it last, in a crowded center or behind a button means many viewers miss the main message.

title: A dashboard with eleven crowded views
question: A sales dashboard packs eleven worksheets onto one screen. Users say they cannot tell what matters and that it loads slowly. Which redesign best follows dashboard best practice?
options: Shrink fonts and legends so all eleven views fit without scrolling
Keep two or three key views and move detail to linked dashboards
Add a tab strip at the top so each view can be shown in turn
Replace every chart with a table so that exact numbers are visible
explanation: Tableau's guidance is to limit a dashboard to two or three views, because each extra view competes for attention and adds queries that slow loading; detail belongs on further dashboards reached through navigation or actions. Shrinking everything keeps the clutter, a tab strip hides the same lack of focus, and tables make patterns harder, not easier, to see.

title: One dashboard for two very different audiences
question: A contact-center floor team must react within minutes to queue spikes, while executives review quarterly service trends. A stakeholder asks for one dashboard containing every metric for both groups. What is the better design?
options: One dashboard with all metrics, refreshed weekly to limit load
One dashboard per group, showing each metric as a sortable table
A near-real-time view for the floor and a trend view for executives
One executive dashboard, with the floor team exporting data to Excel
explanation: Operational and strategic audiences need different metrics, time grains and refresh rates: the floor team needs a few current-state indicators that update continuously, while executives need trends compared with targets. Weekly refresh is useless for the floor team, tables bury the signal, and Excel exports lose the timeliness the operational use case depends on. Knowing your purpose and audience is the first dashboard design step.

title: A report page with forty visuals loads slowly
question: A Power BI report page with 40 visuals takes about 15 seconds to render after every slicer change. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Increase the scheduled refresh frequency of the semantic model
Profile the page and cut visuals, moving detail to drillthrough pages
Convert all of the visuals to tables, which are always the cheapest
Enable bidirectional filtering on every relationship in the model
explanation: Each visual on a page issues its own queries when filters change, so 40 visuals multiply the work; Microsoft recommends limiting visuals per page and using drillthrough pages and report page tooltips for detail, with Performance Analyzer to find the slowest ones. Refresh frequency does not affect render time, tables are often among the most expensive visuals, and bidirectional filters usually add query cost.

title: A 'company total' tile that follows the map filter
question: On a dashboard, clicking a region on the map filters every sheet, including a tile titled 'Company revenue'. Executives start quoting a regional figure as the company total. What is the best fix?
options: Exclude the tile from the action and show active filters in titles
Remove the map so no filtering can happen anywhere on the dashboard
Rename the tile to 'Revenue' so the title fits every selection
Turn the tile into a gauge so that filtered values look different
explanation: Filter actions apply only to the target sheets you choose, so a company-wide KPI can be excluded from the action and stay unfiltered; showing the current selection in titles also makes the filter state visible. Removing the map loses useful interactivity, renaming hides the problem instead of solving it, and a gauge changes the chart type but not the misleading number.

title: A chart title that tells the story
question: You present a chart showing churn dropping after an onboarding redesign in March. Which title best supports a data story?
options: Monthly churn rate from January to December 2026
Churn analysis: an overview of customer retention metrics
Churn fell 30% after the March onboarding redesign
Figure 4: churn rate by month (source: CRM export)
explanation: A headline title that states the takeaway tells the audience what to see and why it matters, while the chart provides the evidence. Descriptive titles such as a date range, a generic label or a figure number are accurate, but they leave each viewer to find (or miss) the conclusion alone.

title: Drawing attention to one series out of eight
question: A line chart shows eight product lines, but your message is about just one of them. What is the most effective way to focus attention?
options: Give each line a distinct bright color so all of them stand out
Make every line thicker so that the chart is easier to read
Add a legend with eight entries ordered by total revenue
Draw the focus line in a strong color and mute the others in gray
explanation: Using neutral colors for context and a single bright color for the key series is a recommended way to emphasize a finding: the eye goes straight to the contrast. Eight bright colors compete equally, a long legend makes viewers decode instead of see, and uniformly thicker lines add weight without creating any emphasis.

title: Status shown only by red and green dots
question: A KPI table marks each metric as on track or off track using only green and red dots. Some viewers have red-green color vision deficiency. What fix best meets accessibility guidance?
options: Swap red and green for orange and teal, keeping dots as the only cue
Add a second cue such as an icon shape or a text label with the color
Raise the saturation of both colors so the difference is more vivid
Explain in a footnote that red means off track and green on track
explanation: WCAG's Use of Color criterion requires that color not be the only visual means of conveying information, so the status needs a redundant cue such as distinct icon shapes or a label. Changing hues or saturation can still fail for some viewers and on grayscale printouts, and a footnote explains the code but still leaves color as the only signal.

title: A headline number with no context
question: In a board update, a slide says only 'Revenue this month: $2.3M' in large type. Board members ask whether that is good or bad. What is missing?
options: A more precise value, such as $2,312,447.18
A larger font and a brand-colored background card
A pie chart breaking the $2.3M down by product
A comparison such as target, prior period or forecast
explanation: A number only becomes meaningful against a reference point: the target, last month, the same month last year or the forecast tells the audience whether to celebrate or worry. Extra decimals add false precision, a breakdown answers a different question, and styling does not provide context.

title: A one-off spike in the middle of the story
question: Monthly sales show a spike in March caused by a single one-off bulk order. You are presenting a forecast built on the trend. What is the most honest way to handle the spike?
options: Silently delete March so the trend line looks smooth and credible
Keep March unmarked and let the audience notice the spike themselves
Annotate the spike, explain it, and say how the forecast handles it
Switch to quarterly totals so that the spike blends into Q1
explanation: Annotation keeps the data visible while explaining why the point is unusual, and stating whether the forecast excludes or includes it lets the audience judge the result. Silently deleting data or hiding it in a coarser aggregate undermines trust once someone notices, and leaving it unexplained invites viewers to draw the wrong conclusion from the spike.

title: Spotting a leading indicator
question: Your team's goal is next quarter's revenue. Which of these metrics is a leading indicator for that goal?
options: Last quarter's recognized revenue
Customers who churned during last year
Annual net profit in the audited report
Qualified pipeline value created this month
explanation: A leading indicator moves before the outcome and can still be influenced, so newly created qualified pipeline predicts future revenue. Recognized revenue, audited profit and last year's churn are lagging indicators: they measure results that have already happened and are useful for evaluation, not for steering early.

title: What turns a number into a KPI
question: A dashboard tile shows 'Average resolution time: 6.2 hours'. What does it most need to work as a KPI rather than just a metric?
options: A target or threshold that defines good versus bad performance
More decimal places so that small changes are visible to viewers
A gauge visual instead of a card so it looks more like a KPI
A drill-down from hours into minutes and seconds for precision
explanation: A KPI evaluates a value against a defined target, so it needs that target (and usually a trend) to show whether performance is on track; Power BI's KPI visual is built from a base measure, a target and a trend axis for exactly this reason. Extra precision, a different visual or finer time units still leave the viewer unable to judge whether 6.2 hours is good.

title: A productivity KPI that backfired
question: After 'tickets closed per agent' became the support team's main KPI, it rose 40% while customer satisfaction fell. Audits show tickets being closed early and then reopened. What is the best response?
options: Raise the target for tickets closed so agents work even faster
Pair it with counter-metrics such as reopen rate and CSAT
Stop measuring support entirely, since any metric gets gamed
Report the KPI less often so that agents feel less pressure
explanation: When a measure becomes a target, people optimize the measure itself (Goodhart's law); balancing it with counter-metrics such as reopen rate, first-contact resolution or CSAT makes gaming visible and keeps quality in view. Raising the target intensifies the gaming, dropping measurement removes visibility, and reporting less often does not change the incentive.

title: Monthly conversion rate built from daily rates
question: A dashboard computes monthly conversion rate as the average of 30 daily rates, giving 4.1%. Total conversions divided by total sessions for the month gives 2.7%. Traffic varies a lot by day. Which number should the KPI report?
options: 4.1%, because averaging the daily rates treats every day fairly
Either one, since both are valid averages of the same daily data
The midpoint, 3.4%, to balance the bias of the two methods
2.7%, because a ratio of totals weights each day by its traffic
explanation: An average of daily ratios gives a low-traffic day the same weight as a busy one, so a few small days with high rates inflate the result; the monthly rate must be `SUM(conversions) / SUM(sessions)` at the reported grain. In BI tools this means defining the KPI as a measure that divides aggregates, not averaging a precomputed ratio column. Averaging the two numbers has no statistical meaning.

title: Summing weekly active users into a month
question: A team reports monthly active users (MAU) by adding up the four weekly active user counts of the month. Many users are active every week. What is wrong, and how should MAU be computed?
options: Nothing; weekly counts are additive as long as the weeks don't overlap
It undercounts; the weekly counts should be multiplied by four instead
Distinct counts aren't additive; count distinct users over the month
It only fails for partial weeks; prorate the first and last weeks instead
explanation: A distinct count is non-additive: a user active in all four weeks is counted four times when weekly results are summed. MAU must be a distinct count over the month's raw activity (Looker's `count_distinct` measure type, DISTINCTCOUNT in DAX, COUNTD in Tableau). Non-overlapping weeks don't help because the same users recur, multiplying makes the overcount worse, and prorating only fixes calendar edges, not the double counting.

title: Why BI tools have a semantic layer
question: Looker's LookML models, Power BI semantic models and Tableau published data sources play a similar role. What is the main purpose of this semantic layer?
options: To keep a second physical copy of the warehouse as a backup
To define joins, metrics and names once so reports reuse them
To replace SQL databases with a faster proprietary file format
To render charts on the server instead of in the user's browser
explanation: A semantic layer sits between raw tables and reports, encoding business logic (relationships, measure definitions, friendly names, security) once so every report and user gets consistent numbers. It is not a backup copy, it does not replace the database (Looker in particular generates SQL that runs in the database), and it has nothing to do with where charts are rendered.

title: Margin % that must respond to every slicer
question: In Power BI, a report needs Profit Margin % that stays correct at any level (year, region, product) and under any slicer selection. How should it be defined?
options: As a calculated column computing Profit / Sales on each row, then averaged
As a calculated column in the Date table that stores each year's margin
As a Power Query column computed during refresh and summed in visuals
As a measure dividing summed profit by summed sales, in filter context
explanation: Measures are evaluated at query time in the current filter context, so `DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Profit]), SUM(Sales[Amount]))` recalculates correctly for whatever slicers and grouping apply. Calculated columns and Power Query columns are computed row by row at refresh; averaging or summing a stored per-row ratio gives wrong totals, and a per-year column cannot respond to region or product filters. The same measure-versus-row-calculation split exists in Tableau and Looker.

title: Dashboard showing yesterday's numbers
question: A Tableau dashboard is built on an extract refreshed nightly. Operations managers complain that during the day they only see yesterday's numbers. What explains this, and what is the trade-off of fixing it?
options: The extract is a snapshot; going live or refreshing more often adds source load
Browser caching hides the new rows; clearing it fixes this with no trade-off
Extracts drop rows above a size limit; splitting the workbook fixes it for free
Dashboards cache data for 24 hours by design; nothing can make them fresher
explanation: An extract is a stored snapshot that is only as current as its last refresh, which is also why it is fast. A live connection or more frequent (incremental) refreshes increase freshness at the cost of more load on the source and potentially slower queries; Power BI's Import versus DirectQuery choice is the same trade-off. Browser caching and size limits do not explain day-old data, and freshness is configurable.

title: FIXED LOD ignores the Category filter
question: In Tableau, `{ FIXED [Region] : SUM([Sales]) }` keeps showing all-category totals even though the user filtered Category to 'Furniture' with a regular dimension filter. How do you make the LOD respect that filter?
options: Apply it as a table calculation filter so it runs later in the pipeline
Add the Category filter to context so it is applied before the LOD
Move the Category field onto the Marks card as Detail instead
Wrap the expression in ATTR() so that it is evaluated after filters
explanation: In Tableau's order of operations, FIXED expressions ignore every filter except context, data source and extract filters, so a regular dimension filter is applied too late to affect them. Adding the Category filter to context moves it ahead of the FIXED calculation. A table calculation filter runs even later, putting Category on Detail changes the view's granularity rather than the filter order, and ATTR() does not change when the LOD is evaluated.

title: Order totals inflated after a one-to-many join
question: In a Looker Explore, `orders` is joined to `order_items` (one order has many items). A sum measure on `orders.total` shows inflated values when item fields are selected. What prevents this fanout error?
options: A unique primary key on `orders` plus the right join relationship
Switching the join type from left_outer to full_outer in the Explore
Changing the measure from type: sum to type: number with a CASE
Adding a datagroup so that the corrected results are cached first
explanation: A one-to-many join repeats each order row once per item, so a naive SUM counts each order total several times. Looker's symmetric aggregates use the view's primary key (together with the declared join relationship) to count each order only once. Changing the join type keeps the fanout, a type: number measure does not de-duplicate anything, and caching only serves the wrong answer faster. Other tools address the same problem through relationship-aware models.

title: What belongs in a fact table
question: In a retail star schema, which set of columns belongs in the sales fact table?
options: Product name, product category, subcategory and brand
Store name, city, region, manager and opening date
Customer name, email address, segment and loyalty tier
Date key, product key, store key, quantity and amount
explanation: Fact tables store measurable events at a declared grain (here, one sale line), holding foreign keys to dimensions plus numeric measures such as quantity and amount. Descriptive attributes used for filtering and grouping, like product category, store region or customer tier, belong in dimension tables.

title: Targets and transactions in one fact table
question: A modeler stores per-transaction sales rows and monthly store targets in the same fact table, leaving blanks where a column does not apply. Report totals are now confusing. Which principle is violated?
options: A fact table should load its data at one consistent grain
A fact table should never contain more than one numeric column
A fact table may relate to at most two dimension tables
Targets must always be stored as attributes of a dimension
explanation: Every fact table should have one declared grain, such as one row per transaction line or one row per store per month; mixing grains makes sums and counts blend unrelated rows. The fix is two fact tables (sales and targets) that share conformed dimensions like Date and Store. Facts are where numeric measures live, there is no two-dimension limit, and targets are measures too, just at a coarser grain.

title: Keeping history when a customer moves
question: A customer moved from São Paulo to Rio de Janeiro in June. Analysts want sales before June to stay attributed to São Paulo and later sales to Rio. Which dimension design supports this?
options: Type 1 SCD: overwrite the city so the dimension is always current
Delete the customer and recreate it with the original natural key
Store the customer's city as a numeric measure in the sales fact
Type 2 SCD: add a new row with a new surrogate key and validity dates
explanation: A Type 2 slowly changing dimension versions the member: the old row keeps São Paulo, a new row (new surrogate key, with effective dates and often a current flag) holds Rio, and each fact points to the version valid when it happened. Type 1 overwrites, rewriting history so all past sales move to Rio. Turning a text attribute into a measure or recreating the customer breaks the model and loses the history.

title: Order, ship and delivery dates on one fact
question: A sales fact has OrderDate, ShipDate and DeliveryDate, all related to one Date dimension in a Power BI model. Only the OrderDate relationship works in visuals. How do you also analyze by ship date?
options: Unpivot the three date columns into one column with a date-type flag
Set all three relationships to active and bidirectional at the same time
Activate it in a measure with USERELATIONSHIP, or add a Ship Date table
Drop the Date dimension and group visuals by the raw fact date columns
explanation: Date is a role-playing dimension here. Power BI allows only one active filter path between two tables, so the other relationships are inactive; a measure can activate one with `USERELATIONSHIP`, or you can load a separate Ship Date table so each role has its own active relationship. Multiple active paths are not allowed, unpivoting triples the fact rows, and dropping the dimension loses attributes such as fiscal periods and time intelligence.

title: Bidirectional filters on every relationship
question: To 'make slicers work everywhere', a modeler set every relationship in a multi-fact star schema to bidirectional. Now some totals are wrong, some relationships cannot be activated because of ambiguous paths, and reports are slower. What is the recommended approach?
options: Keep bidirectional filtering, but convert every relationship to many-to-many
Merge all the fact tables into a single wide table to remove ambiguity
Filter one-way from dimensions to facts; go bidirectional only when needed
Replace the relationships with calculated columns that look up the keys
explanation: Microsoft's guidance is to keep relationships single-direction (dimensions filter facts) and enable bidirectional filtering only for specific needs, because it can create ambiguous filter paths, unexpected results and slower queries; when one calculation needs it, `CROSSFILTER` inside a measure limits the effect. Many-to-many relationships, a single wide table or lookup columns trade this problem for bigger ones in correctness, model size or maintainability.
